topic: git push --force-with-lease vs --force, and why --force-if-includes closes the background-fetch gap
text:
Stop typing `git push --force` after a rebase. There's a safer default.

--force overwrites the remote branch no matter what is on it. If a teammate pushed a commit while you were rebasing, it's gone.

--force-with-lease only overwrites if the remote branch is still where your remote-tracking ref says it is. Otherwise the push fails.

The catch, straight from the Git docs: if anything runs `git fetch` in the background (an IDE, a cron job), your tracking ref updates without you ever seeing the new commits, and the lease check passes anyway.

The fix is one extra flag:

git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes

It also checks that the remote tip is reachable from your local branch's reflog, meaning you've actually integrated it.

Takeaway: --force says "I don't care what's there." The lease says "only if nothing changed."

Do you alias a safe force-push in your team, or ban force-pushing altogether?
